anomaly_def.Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Composite definition: The database instance is simultaneously mis-configured at the parameter level, constrained by an overstressed transaction-log subsystem, and suffering from host CPU saturation. The three root causes coexist and interact, so the platform is neither tuned for the hardware nor able to absorb the log-write volume it produces, while CPU time is exhausted trying to keep up with both normal workload processing and log-related background activity.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Commit latency and log-flush waits rise sharply even when underlying storage metrics show spare IOPS; 2) Checkpoint storms, frequent log-file switches, and growing archive backlogs coincide with OS run-queue spikes and near-100 % CPU utilization; 3) Wait-event views show an interleaving of log-write, CPU scheduler, and configuration-driven background worker waits; 4) After a parameter change or version upgrade, throughput falls off cliff-like, with application threads alternately spinning on CPU and blocking on log-sync, while monitoring tools report buffer pools or per-session work memory either overcommitted or too small; 5) Secondary symptoms such as replication lag, autovacuum/cleanup backlog, and plan-cache thrashing become harder to attribute to a single layer because every mitigation attempt (e.g., raising parallelism or lowering checkpoint frequency) quickly pushes the system into a different but equally constrained state.

Causal chain and interaction: Poorly chosen configuration parameters (e.g., undersized log buffer, aggressive synchronous-commit, or checkpoint-completion target set too low) increase the frequency and immediacy of log flushes. This drives the transaction-log subsystem toward its throughput limit; once the log path slows, foreground sessions hold latches longer and CPU spin-time rises, inflating overall CPU utilization. The elevated CPU demand further delays log-writer and archiver threads, deepening log congestion. Meanwhile, CPU saturation prevents background processes from performing adaptive tuning or deferred I/O, so configuration mis-matches (such as small buffer pools or excessive parallel workers) cannot self-correct and instead generate even more redo. The feedback loop—mis-configuration → log pressure → CPU thrashing → slower log processing—amplifies each individual anomaly, producing a compounded failure mode that is more severe and harder to diagnose than any of the three issues in isolation.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the timeout in seconds for attempts to acquire metadata locks.
entry.trigger_condition: A statement waits longer than lock_wait_timeout while attempting to acquire a metadata lock.
entry.workload_impact: The metadata lock acquisition fails and the statement does not proceed.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
